usage: to be responsible / to bear responsibility
the core stative pattern; the duty rests on you (책임이 없다 = it's not on you)
fixed phrase with 지다 (to carry on the back); this is how you say you'll own the outcome
add 감(感, feeling) to name the inner trait; describes a person, not the duty itself
add 자(者, person) for the responsible party, e.g. the manager handling an issue
examples: 그건 제 책임이에요.
That's my responsibility.
simplest form: 책임 + 이에요 to flatly claim a duty as yours
부모는 아이에 대한 책임이 있어요.
Parents have a responsibility toward their children.
N에 대한 책임 marks who or what the responsibility is for
이 일은 제가 맡았으니까 끝까지 책임을 지겠습니다.
Since I took on this work, I will take responsibility for it to the end.
formal 합니다 form with 책임을 지다; common at work when committing to a task
nuance: 책임 (責任, 責 'demand/blame' + 任 'duty entrusted') is the abstract weight of being answerable for an outcome, and it lives almost entirely through verbs: 책임을 지다 (shoulder it) and 책임이 있다 (it falls on you). The dividing line you must learn is 책임 vs 의무: 책임 is accountability AFTER the fact (who answers if it goes wrong), while 의무 is a duty you are required to perform regardless of result. Also distinguish the bare noun 책임 from 책임감, which is the inner sense of duty a person feels, so describe an obligation with 책임 but a person's character with 책임감. The classic English-speaker trap is treating 책임 like the verb 'to be responsible' and saying 책임하다; Korean has no such verb, so you must reach for 책임을 지다 or 책임이 있다.

Avoid 책임을 가지다 (a 직역 of 'have responsibility'); the natural collocation is 책임이 있다 with the subject particle 이, not 가지다.

usage: to have an obligation / to be obligated
the standard pattern; pairs with -아/어야 한다 ideas of 'must'
fixed phrase with 다하다 (to do fully); sounds formal and earnest
N의 의무 names a specific civic duty; one of the constitutional 4대 의무
의무 + 적 + 으로 makes the adverb for things you must do, not by choice
examples: 교육은 국민의 의무예요.
Education is a duty of citizens.
simplest N은/는 N의 의무 frame stating a flat civic duty
저는 제 의무를 다했을 뿐이에요.
I only fulfilled my duty.
modest reply when thanked; 의무를 다하다 + -았을 뿐이다 (nothing more)
이 교육은 의무적으로 들어야 해요.
You have to take this training as a requirement.
의무적으로 stresses it is mandatory; pairs naturally with -아/어야 하다
nuance: 의무 (義務, 義 'righteousness/what is right' + 務 'task') is a duty imposed from OUTSIDE, by law, rule, or role, that you are required to carry out, and it is the natural opposite of 권리 (rights) — the pair 권리와 의무 is almost a set phrase. The boundary against 책임 is the key one for learners: 의무 is the binding requirement to act (you MUST), while 책임 is being answerable once something is done or goes wrong. It feels distinctly more formal and rule-bound than 책임, so you'll meet 의무 in civic contexts like taxes (납세), military service (국방), and compulsory education. The English-speaker pitfall is using 의무 for a casual favor: because English 'I'm obligated to' can be loose, learners overreach, but 의무 implies a genuinely binding requirement, so a friendly request is never an 의무.

Avoid saying 의무하다; 의무 is a noun, so use 의무가 있다 or 의무를 다하다 to express the action.

usage: the core pattern; states an entitlement you are owed (권리가 없다 = you have no claim)
주장하다 (to claim/insist); used when standing up for what you are owed
기본(基本) + 권리 for fundamental rights; 기본권 is the compressed legal term
보호하다 (to protect); appears in formal, legal, and consumer contexts
examples: 저도 알 권리가 있어요.
I have a right to know too.
simple V-(으)ㄹ 권리가 있다; everyday way to assert an entitlement
소비자는 자신의 권리를 잘 알아야 해요.
Consumers should know their rights well.
common in consumer education; 권리 as the noun object of 알다
권리에는 항상 의무가 따라요.
Obligations always follow rights.
권리 and 의무 paired as opposites; 권리에는 ... 따르다 is a stock saying
nuance: 권리 (權利, 權 'authority/power' + 利 'benefit') is a right in the sense of a justly-owed entitlement you may claim, and it is the structural partner of 의무 (duty) — they are introduced together as 권리와 의무. The synonym line to watch is 권리 vs 권한: 권리 is what an individual is OWED (a citizen's right to vote), whereas 권한(權限) is delegated AUTHORITY to act within limits (a manager's authority to approve), so don't say a boss has 권리 to sign off — that's 권한. A pronunciation note: 권리 surfaces as [궐리] because ㄴ assimilates to ㄹ next to 리. The big English-speaker pitfall is the false friend with direction: 권리 never means 'right' as in right-versus-left — that is 오른쪽 — so 'turn right' is 오른쪽으로, never 권리.

Do not mix up 권리 (what you're owed) with 권한 (authority delegated to act); a manager's sign-off power is 권한, not 권리.

usage: the most common description; 강하다 (strong) vs 약하다 (weak)
used to admit you give in easily, e.g. on a diet or quitting smoking
add 력(力, power) to emphasize will as raw strength against temptation
to have the will to do something
V-(으)ㄹ 의지가 있다 shows the determination to actually act
examples: 저는 의지가 약해요.
I have weak willpower.
simplest 의지가 약하다; a common half-joking confession before a diet
그 사람은 의지가 강해서 끝까지 포기하지 않았어요.
That person has a strong will, so they didn't give up to the end.
explaining a result with 의지가 강하다 + -아/어서
저는 한국어를 끝까지 배울 의지가 있어요.
I have the will to learn Korean to the end.
V-(으)ㄹ 의지가 있다 expressing firm personal determination
nuance: 의지 (意志, 意 'intention' + 志 'aspiration/resolve') is willpower — the inner resolve to push through difficulty — and it is overwhelmingly described as 강하다 (strong) or 약하다 (weak). The contrast to draw is 의지 vs 의욕(意慾): 의지 is the steady RESOLVE to endure and not quit (의지가 강하다), while 의욕 is the eager DRIVE or motivation to start (의욕이 넘치다, brimming with enthusiasm), so a person can have 의욕 to begin yet lack the 의지 to finish. Because it implies effort against temptation or hardship, 의지 is wrong for a light wish — wanting a snack is never 의지. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is the homophone trap: the noun 의지 (will) looks identical to the verb stem in 의지하다, but 의지하다 means 'to lean on / rely on someone' — a completely different idea — so 친구에게 의지하다 is 'lean on a friend,' not 'will a friend.'

usage: to be frazzled / too busy to think straight
very common idiom; means overwhelmed/swamped, not literally mindless
to pull oneself together / come to one's senses
fixed phrase; snap back to focus or regain composure after a shock
정신 + 적(的): 정신적 스트레스 (mental stress), as opposed to 육체적 (physical)
adverb; doing something so busily you lose all track of time
examples: 요즘 정신이 없어요.
These days I'm swamped.
the everyday meaning of 정신이 없다: overwhelmed, not insane
놀라지 말고 정신 차리세요.
Don't panic and pull yourself together.
정신(을) 차리다 said to someone flustered or in shock; 을 often dropped in speech
몸도 중요하지만 정신 건강도 챙겨야 해요.
The body matters, but you also have to take care of mental health.
정신 건강 (mental health) explicitly contrasted with 몸 (body)
nuance: 정신 (精神, 精 'refined essence/vital energy' + 神 'spirit') spans spirit, mind, and mental clarity, and in daily speech it lives mostly inside idioms you should memorize as whole chunks: 정신이 없다 means too busy or flustered to focus, and 정신을 차리다 means to regain composure. The synonym boundary that trips learners is 정신 vs 마음: 정신 leans toward mental FOCUS, alertness, and consciousness (the cognitive faculty), while 마음 is the heart — feelings, intentions, and emotional warmth — so 마음이 아프다 is 'heartbroken' but 정신이 아프다 is not idiomatic. It also contrasts with 몸 (body) in 정신 건강 (mental health). The English-speaker pitfall is reading 정신이 없다 literally as 'has no mind/is mindless'; it actually means frazzled or swamped, so never translate these idioms word by word.

usage: 상상 + 하다 makes the transitive verb; picture a scene in your mind
the high-frequency idiom; 상상이 되다 = it's imaginable, 안 되다 = it isn't
add 력(力, power) for the faculty of imagination, often praised in children
fixed phrase: 상상 + 이상(以上, above) + 으로, meaning far more than expected
examples: 상상도 못 했어요.
I couldn't have even imagined it.
compact 상상도 못 하다 for total surprise; 도 adds 'even'
그 영화가 얼마나 무서웠는지 상상이 안 돼요.
You can't imagine how scary that movie was.
상상이 안 되다 is the natural way to say 'unimaginable'
결과가 상상 이상으로 좋았어요.
The result was better than I imagined.
상상 이상으로 stresses exceeding all expectation
nuance: 상상 (想像, 想 'think/conceive' + 像 'image') is imagination — forming pictures or hypothetical scenarios in the mind — and it becomes a verb as 상상하다. The synonym line is 상상 vs 생각: 상상 specifically conjures something UNREAL, hypothetical, or not-yet-experienced (picturing life on Mars), while 생각 is ordinary thinking, opinion, or recollection, so 'I think it's true' is 생각, never 상상. The single most useful everyday chunk is 상상이 안 되다 (I can't even picture it), used for things too extreme or surprising to grasp; for a person's creative capacity use 상상력. The English-speaker pitfall is the negative form: learners model 'I can't imagine' on English and produce 상상이 없다, but Korean treats it as the process failing, so it must be 상상이 안 되다 (it won't come into image), not 없다.

usage: 판단 + 하다; to weigh a situation and form a conclusion
to make a judgment / reach a decision
fixed phrase with 내리다 (to hand down); sounds deliberate and weighty
add 력(力, power) for the ability to judge well: 판단력이 뛰어나다
올바르다 (to be upright/right) + 판단; common in advice and reflection
examples: 판단하기 어려워요.
It's hard to judge.
simplest 판단하다 + -기 어렵다 when you can't yet form a conclusion
성급하게 판단하지 말고 끝까지 들어 보세요.
Don't judge hastily; hear it out to the end.
common advice; 성급하게 판단하다 (to judge rashly) as the thing to avoid
최종 판단은 본인이 내려야 해요.
You have to make the final judgment yourself.
판단을 내리다 for arriving at a weighty decision
nuance: 판단 (判斷, 判 'discern/divide' + 斷 'cut/decide') is the mental act of weighing a situation and forming a reasoned conclusion — the assessment step that comes BEFORE acting. The boundary learners must hold is 판단 vs 결정: 판단 emphasizes the REASONING and evaluation ('is this safe?'), while 결정(決定) is the final CHOICE that follows ('then I'll go'), so a doctor makes a 판단 about your condition and you make the 결정 to have surgery. It collocates with 내리다 as 판단을 내리다 (hand down a judgment), and 판단력 names the skill of judging well. The English-speaker pitfall is overusing 판단 for ordinary 'decide': everyday choices like picking a restaurant are 결정하다 or 정하다, while 판단 carries a heavier, analytical, almost evaluative tone — and note the verb is 판단하다, never 판단이 하다 or 판단을 하다 in neutral use.

usage: fixed phrase with 세우다 (to set up/erect); how you establish an aim
이루다 (to accomplish); reaching what you aimed for (also 달성하다)
정하다 (to fix/settle); pinning down exactly what you'll aim for
to aim for / set as a goal
N을/를 목표로 하다 marks the target you work toward
examples: 제 목표는 합격이에요.
My goal is to pass.
simplest 제 목표는 N(이)에요 frame for stating an aim
작은 목표부터 하나씩 이루어 나가고 있어요.
I'm achieving them one by one, starting from small goals.
목표를 이루다 + -아 나가다 for steady ongoing progress
TOPIK 3급 합격을 목표로 공부하고 있어요.
I'm studying with the goal of passing TOPIK level 3.
N을/를 목표로 marks the concrete target you aim for
nuance: 목표 (目標, 目 'eye' + 標 'mark/sign' — literally the mark the eye fixes on) is a concrete, measurable goal or target you aim at, and it travels with a tight verb family: 세우다 or 정하다 to set it, 이루다 or 달성하다 to achieve it. The synonym line is 목표 vs 꿈: 목표 is specific and outcome-focused (pass TOPIK 3, save 1,000,000 won, run 5km), while 꿈 is broader, emotional, and aspirational (become a doctor, a better world), so use 목표 for things you can tick off and 꿈 for the life vision behind them. Note also 목표 vs 목적(目的): 목표 is the concrete TARGET, 목적 is the underlying PURPOSE/reason. The English-speaker pitfall is forming a verb directly: 'to goal' tempts learners into 목표하다, which is unnatural in writing — say 목표를 세우다 or 목표로 하다 instead.

usage: 첫 (first) + 인상; the impression you make on first meeting
describes how someone comes across in looks or manner (인상이 나쁘다 = off-putting)
인상(이) 깊다 = it left a deep impression; 깊다 literally 'deep'
좋은 인상을 주다 = to make a good impression on someone
examples: 인상이 참 좋으시네요.
You give such a nice impression.
인상이 좋다 as a warm compliment about someone's manner; honorific -으시-
면접에서는 첫인상이 정말 중요해요.
First impressions are really important in interviews.
첫인상 in a practical, high-stakes context
그 영화는 결말이 인상 깊었어요.
That movie's ending was very memorable.
인상(이) 깊다 for something that stuck with you
nuance: 인상 (印象, 印 'stamp/imprint' + 象 'image' — literally an image stamped on the mind) is the impression a person or thing leaves on you, and it surfaces mostly in 첫인상 (first impression), 인상이 좋다 (comes across well), and 인상(이) 깊다 (memorable). The synonym line is 인상 vs 느낌: 인상 is the overall IMPRESSION someone gives others (often judged from appearance and manner: 인상이 좋다), while 느낌 is the subjective FEELING/vibe YOU personally get ('I got a weird feeling'), so 첫인상 is what you project, 느낌 is what you sense. The big English-speaker pitfall is the homophone with economics: 인상 also means a price/wage HIKE (가격 인상, 인상되다), a totally separate word, so 'a deep impression' is 인상이 깊다 but '가격이 인상되다' is 'the price was raised' — context disambiguates, and 인상 깊다 must never be read literally as 'a deep face.'

Do not swap 인상 with 느낌: 인상 is the impression you give others, while 느낌 is the personal feeling/vibe you receive.

usage: says someone has moral sense; the negative 양심이 없다 is a harsh insult
to feel a pang of conscience / guilty
fixed idiom with 찔리다 (to be pricked/stabbed); a guilty twinge inside
양심 + 적(的): 양심적인 사람 = a person who acts on conscience
to keep one's conscience / stay honest
지키다 (to keep/guard); to act rightly even when no one is watching
examples: 저는 양심에 찔려요.
My conscience bothers me.
bare 양심에 찔리다; the everyday way to admit you feel guilty
그분은 양심적으로 일하는 분이에요.
That person works conscientiously.
양심적으로 (adverb) for acting with honest integrity
아무도 안 봐도 양심을 지키는 게 중요해요.
Even if no one is watching, keeping your conscience matters.
양심을 지키다 for staying honest unobserved
nuance: 양심 (良心, 良 'good' + 心 'heart/mind' — literally 'the good heart') is the conscience, your inner sense of right and wrong, and it surfaces in the idiom 양심에 찔리다 (to feel a twinge of guilt) and the adjective 양심적 (conscientious). The synonym line is 양심 vs 의식(意識): 양심 is the MORAL faculty that judges right from wrong and produces guilt, while 의식 is AWARENESS/consciousness in the cognitive or social sense (의식을 잃다 'lose consciousness'; 환경 의식 'environmental awareness'), so a guilty pang is 양심, not 의식. The crucial register caution — the English-speaker pitfall here — is that 양심이 없다 ('to have no conscience') is NOT a neutral remark like English 'unscrupulous'; it is a strong moral insult meaning shameless or brazen (often heard as 양심 없다!), so deploy it carefully and never casually about a colleague.

usage: 기억 + 하다; the transitive verb for deliberately remembering
fixed phrase with 나다 (to arise); the memory surfaces on its own
the everyday way to say it slipped your mind (not a refusal)
to stay in one's memory / be memorable
남다 (to remain); something you won't forget
examples: 기억이 안 나요.
I can't remember.
the default, natural way to say something slipped your mind
그날 일을 아직도 똑똑히 기억하고 있어요.
I still clearly remember what happened that day.
active 기억하다 + -고 있다 = deliberately holding it in mind, unlike the passive 기억이 나다
어릴 때 살던 동네가 아직도 기억에 남아 있어요.
The neighborhood I lived in as a child still stays in my memory.
기억에 남다 (+ -아 있다) for a lasting, vivid memory
nuance: 기억 (記憶, 記 'record/write down' + 憶 'recall/think of') is memory or recollection, and the key intermediate skill is choosing the idiom over the bare verb. The contrast learners must internalize is 기억하다 vs 기억이 나다: 기억하다 is ACTIVE, deliberate holding-in-mind ('be sure to remember this', 꼭 기억하세요), while 기억이 나다 is the memory PASSIVELY surfacing on its own ('oh, it just came back to me'), so 'I can't recall' is the spontaneous 기억이 안 나다, not the deliberate-sounding 기억하지 않다. 기억에 남다 describes something that stays with you. There is also a synonym boundary against 추억(追憶): 추억 is specifically FOND, nostalgic memory of the past (good old days), so warm childhood memories can be 추억, but a phone number you forgot is only 기억. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'don't remember' to 기억하지 않다, which wrongly implies a willful choice not to remember.

mistakes: For 'can't remember,' use 기억이 안 나다, not the stiff 기억하지 않다 — the latter implies a deliberate refusal to remember.
